::: {.callout-important}
## This is not a diagnostic tool

Nothing here can tell you whether a lesion is dangerous. If something on your
skin concerns you, see a doctor. That is the whole point of this project, and
the rest of it is an argument for why.
:::

## What this project is

I trained a small neural network to classify skin lesions from dermatoscopic
images, using the HAM10000 dataset [@tschandl2018ham10000]. It is a learning
project. The model is modest and the results are honest rather than impressive:
on a seven-class problem it reaches a balanced accuracy of 0.69, where guessing
would score 0.14.

More usefully, it misses about two melanomas in five, and calls roughly one in
five of them an ordinary mole.

I have written up the whole thing rather than only the parts that worked. The
three chapters that follow cover what is in the dataset and what is awkward
about it, every stage of the pipeline and why each decision was made, and what
the trained model actually does. The reasoning matters more than the number.

## The name

HAM10000 stands for *Human Against Machine with 10000 training images*
[@tschandl2018ham10000]. The dataset was assembled with the comparison in mind,
and the [challenge chapter](book/challenge.qmd) makes it literal: you are shown a
lesion, you say melanoma or mole, and the network answers the same question at
the same moment, running in your browser.

Most people do not beat it by much. That is the interesting part, and it cuts
in a direction people do not expect.

## Why a bad classifier still makes the point {#sec-clinician}

It would be easy to read a mediocre model as a reason for scepticism about the
technology. I think the opposite conclusion is available, and more useful.

If a small network trained on ten thousand images can hold its own against you,
then your own unaided judgement about a mark on your skin is not worth much
either. Neither of you should be making this call.

And a dermatologist is not doing a better version of what either of you just
did. Looking at a photograph of a lesion is a fraction of the actual task.
A dermatologist:

- examines the lesion under magnification with a dermatoscope, in person, with
  control over lighting and angle;
- knows your history, your family history, your skin type, your history of
  sunburn;
- can see the rest of your skin, and judge whether a lesion looks different
  from your other lesions, which is often the informative comparison;
- palpates it, and asks whether it has changed, itched, or bled;
- can photograph it and look again in three months, so that change over time
  becomes evidence;
- and when unsure, does not have to decide at all. They biopsy, and the
  question is settled by a pathologist.

That last point is the one an image classifier cannot reach. The model must
answer. A clinician can say *I do not know yet, let us find out*, and then find
out.

## How to read this

Each chapter stands alone.
[Exploration](notebooks/00_exploration.ipynb) is about the dataset and needs no machine
learning background. [The pipeline](notebooks/01_pipeline.ipynb) is the technical core.
[Results](notebooks/02_results.ipynb) is what the model does and what it fails at.
[The challenge](book/challenge.qmd) is the game.

The code is on [GitHub](https://github.com/tmfreiberg/human-against-machine),
along with a command-line tool that reproduces every figure and table here.
